title: How to Solve Grade 4 Word Problems: A Step-by-Step Method (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: How to Solve Grade 4 Word Problems (Method + Quiz)
meta_desc: Learn how to solve Grade 4 word problems with one repeatable 7-step method for mixed, multi-step sums. Includes a free quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Most Grade 4 kids can add and multiply just fine — they lose marks because they pick the wrong operation, or stop after one step when the problem needed two. Here is the general method I teach, plus a quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a scene every Grade 4 parent knows. Your child reads ‘Riya bought 3 boxes of sweets with 24 sweets in each box and gave away 15,’ grabs the two numbers they spot first — 3 and 15 — and writes 3 + 15 = 18. The arithmetic is perfect. The answer is wrong. That gap is exactly what this guide is about: how to solve Grade 4 word problems by choosing the right operation, in the right order, instead of guessing from whichever numbers jump off the page.

By Grade 4 the sums themselves are not the hard part. Most children can add four-digit numbers and multiply 24 × 3 without blinking. What trips them up is the thinking before the calculating — and, more than anything, the fact that a Grade 4 problem very often hides a second step. Master a single reliable process and the marks come back.

The 7-step method for any Grade 4 word problem

This is the routine I drill until it becomes automatic. It works for addition, subtraction, multiplication and division equally, which is the whole point — you should not need a different plan for each.

  • Read it twice. The first read is for the story; the second is for the numbers. Never solve on the first read.
  • Underline the question. What is it actually asking for — a total, a difference, how many in each group, how many left over?
  • List the knowns. Write the given numbers with their units in the margin: 3 boxes, 24 per box, 15 given away.
  • Choose the operation(s). Decide what each number is doing to the others. This is where most marks are won or lost.
  • Estimate first. A quick rounded guess (about 3 × 25 = 75, minus 15, so near 60) tells you instantly if the final answer is sensible.
  • Solve step by step. Show each line. 24 × 3 = 72, then 72 − 15 = 57.
  • Check against the question. Re-read what was asked and confirm your number answers that, with the right unit.

Choosing the right operation

Step 4 deserves its own section, because it is where children freeze. Instead of hunting for keywords, ask what is happening to the quantities. Combining groups? Add. Taking away or comparing? Subtract. Equal groups repeated? Multiply. Sharing or splitting into equal parts? Divide. Here is the map I put on the wall.

What the story is doingOperationGrade 4 example
Putting groups togetherAddition1,245 + 878 books in two libraries
Taking away or finding the differenceSubtraction500 − 275 rupees left after shopping
Equal groups, repeatedMultiplication18 rows of 12 chairs
Sharing equally or making equal groupsDivision96 laddoos into 8 boxes

Why clue words can betray you

You have probably heard the trick: ‘altogether means add, left means subtract.’ It works often enough to be dangerous. Consider: ‘Aarav has 40 stickers altogether, shared equally in 5 albums.’ The word is altogether, but the operation is division. Clue words are hints, not instructions. Teach your child to treat them as a nudge to re-read, never as permission to stop thinking. In my experience, the children who lean hardest on keyword tricks are the ones who plateau in Grade 5, because the problems there are built to punish exactly that shortcut.

The hidden second step

This is the single biggest reason a confident Grade 4 child loses marks. Multi-step problems look like one-step problems until you check the question. ‘A shopkeeper buys 6 crates of 40 mangoes and 55 mangoes go bad. How many can he sell?’ A child who stops at 6 × 40 = 240 has done real work and still scores zero, because the question asked how many he can sell — that needs 240 − 55 = 185.

How to catch the second step

Train one habit: after solving, re-read the question and ask ‘have I answered this, or just done a calculation the problem set up?’ If your intermediate answer is a stepping stone rather than the thing asked, another step is waiting. Estimating early helps here too — if your estimate was ‘about 185’ and you wrote 240, the mismatch flags the missing step.

A worked mixed example

Let us run the full method on one problem. ‘A school orders 8 packets of 25 notebooks. It keeps 60 and shares the rest equally among 4 classes. How many notebooks per class?’

  • Question: notebooks per class.
  • Knowns: 8 packets, 25 per packet, 60 kept, 4 classes.
  • Operations: multiply, then subtract, then divide — three steps.
  • Estimate: about 8 × 25 = 200, minus 60 is 140, split 4 ways is roughly 35.
  • Solve: 8 × 25 = 200; 200 − 60 = 140; 140 ÷ 4 = 35.
  • Check: 35 per class, matches the estimate. Done.

Notice the estimate did quiet, useful work at the end — it confirmed 35 was sensible without any extra effort.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering mixed and multi-step Grade 4 problems across all four operations. Let your child solve each one on paper using the seven steps, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When you want longer graded practice, the printable mixed word-problems worksheet at the end gives dozens of problems with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Mixed Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight word problems across addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, including multi-step ones. Solve each on paper using the seven steps, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 4 mixed and multi-step word problems

questions.q: Riya buys 3 boxes with 24 sweets in each and gives away 15. How many sweets does she have left?
questions.explanation: Two steps. First multiply: 24 × 3 = 72. Then subtract the 15 given away: 72 − 15 = 57.

questions.q: A shopkeeper has 500 rupees. He spends 145 and then 90 more. How much is left?
questions.explanation: Add the two amounts spent: 145 + 90 = 235. Then subtract from 500: 500 − 235 = 265 rupees.

questions.q: 96 laddoos are packed equally into 8 boxes. How many laddoos are in each box?
questions.explanation: This is equal sharing, so divide: 96 ÷ 8 = 12 laddoos per box.

questions.q: A hall has 18 rows of 12 chairs. How many chairs are there in total?
questions.explanation: Equal groups repeated means multiply: 18 × 12 = 216 chairs.

questions.q: Aarav has 40 stickers shared equally in 5 albums. How many stickers are in each album?
questions.explanation: The word altogether is a trap here. Sharing equally means divide: 40 ÷ 5 = 8 per album.

questions.q: A farmer picks 6 crates of 40 mangoes. If 55 mangoes go bad, how many can he sell?
questions.explanation: Multiply first: 6 × 40 = 240. The question asks how many he can sell, so subtract the bad ones: 240 − 55 = 185.

questions.q: A school orders 8 packets of 25 notebooks, keeps 60, and shares the rest equally among 4 classes. How many notebooks per class?
questions.explanation: Three steps. 8 × 25 = 200; then 200 − 60 = 140; then 140 ÷ 4 = 35 per class.

questions.q: Two libraries have 1,245 and 878 books. About how many books is that altogether?
questions.explanation: Estimate first by rounding: 1,200 + 900 is about 2,100. The exact total, 2,123, confirms it.

faq.q: Why does my child pick the wrong operation even though the maths is easy for them?
faq.a: Because they choose based on the numbers they notice first, or on a keyword, instead of on what the story is doing. Teach them to ask ‘are groups being combined, taken away, repeated, or shared?’ and pick the operation from that, not from the words.

faq.q: How do I know if a Grade 4 word problem is multi-step?
faq.a: Re-read the question after solving and check whether your answer is the thing asked or just a stepping stone. If you found a total but the question wanted ‘how many left’ or ‘how many each’, another step is hiding. Grade 4 problems commonly have two steps.

faq.q: Are keyword tricks like ‘altogether means add’ a good idea?
faq.a: Use them only as a hint to re-read, never as a rule. ‘Shared equally altogether’ contains the word altogether but needs division. Children who rely on keywords tend to stall in Grade 5 when problems are written to defeat that shortcut.

faq.q: Why should my child estimate before solving?
faq.a: A rounded guess takes seconds and acts as a safety net. If the estimate says about 60 and the child writes 18, the mismatch flags a wrong operation or a missing step before any marks are lost.
